chapters.title: Problema I — Is there a Teleological Suspension of the Ethical?
paragraphs: The ethical, as such, is the universal, and as the universal it is that which is valid for every man — which from another side may be expressed thus, that it is valid at every moment. It reposes immanent in itself, hath nothing without it which is its τέλος, but is itself τέλος for everything which it has without it; and when the ethical hath taken this up into itself, it goes no further. Determined as immediate, sensuous, and psychic being, the single individual is the single individual who hath his τέλος in the universal; and this is his ethical task: continually to express himself in this, to abolish his singularity in order to become the universal. As soon as the single individual would assert himself in his singularity over against the universal, he sinneth, and only by acknowledging this can he be reconciled again with the universal. Every time the single individual, after having entered into the universal, feeleth a prompting to assert himself as the single individual, he is in spiritual trial, out of which he worketh himself only by repenting and giving up himself, as the single individual, into the universal. If this be the highest that may be said of man and of his existence, then the ethical hath the same character as a man's eternal blessedness, which through all eternity and at every moment is his τέλος, since it would be a contradiction that it could be given up (i.e., teleologically suspended) — for as soon as it is suspended it is forfeit, whereas that which is suspended is not forfeit, but precisely preserved in the higher, which is its τέλος.

If such be the case, then is Hegel in the right when in the chapter on the Good and Conscience he allows man to be determined only as the single individual; he is in the right to regard this determination as a “moral form of evil” (cf. especially the Philosophy of Right), which must be abolished in the teleology of the ethical, so that the single individual who remaineth in this stage either sinneth or lieth in spiritual trial. What Hegel hath not the right to do, however, is to speak of faith — wrong in not protesting loudly and audibly that Abraham enjoys honor and glory as a father of faith, when he ought rather to be sent home and banished as a murderer.

For faith is precisely this paradox, that the single individual is higher than the universal — yet, mark well, in such a way that the movement repeats itself, that, having been in the universal, he then, as the single individual, isolates himself as higher than the universal. If this be not faith, then is Abraham lost; then hath faith never been in the world, precisely because it hath always been. For if the ethical, that is, the moral, be the highest, and there remain in man nothing incommensurable in any other way than that this incommensurable is evil, that is, the single, which is to be expressed in the universal, then one needeth no other categories than those which Greek philosophy possessed, or those which by consistent thinking may be drawn out of these. This Hegel ought not to have concealed; for he hath, after all, had Greek studies.

One heareth not seldom men who, in default of losing themselves in studies, lose themselves in phrases, declaring that over the Christian world there shineth a light, while a darkness broodeth over heathendom. This kind of talk hath always seemed to me strange, since to this day every more thorough thinker, every more earnest artist, reneweth his youth in the eternal youth of the Greek people. Such an utterance is to be explained by the fact that one knoweth not what one ought to say, but only that one must say something. It is in order that one should say that heathendom did not have faith; but if by this saying one is to have said something, one must be a little more in the clear about what one understandeth by faith, since otherwise one sinketh back into such phrases. To explain the whole of existence, faith and all, without having any conception of what faith is, is easy; and he calculateth not the worst in life who reckoneth upon admiration when he hath such an explanation in hand: for it is as Boileau saith, un sot trouve toujours un plus sot, qui l'admire.

Faith is precisely this paradox, that the single individual as the single individual is higher than the universal, is justified over against it, not subordinate but superior — yet, mark well, in such a way that it is the single individual who, after having been as the single individual subordinated to the universal, now through the universal becometh the single individual who, as the single individual, is superior to it; that the single individual as the single individual standeth in an absolute relation to the absolute. This standpoint will not let itself be mediated; for all mediation taketh place precisely by virtue of the universal; it is, and remaineth in all eternity, a paradox, inaccessible to thought. And yet faith is this paradox — or else (these are the consequences which I would beg the reader to bear in mente at every point, even though it would be too prolix for me to set them down everywhere) — or else there hath never been faith, precisely because it hath always been; or else Abraham is lost.

That this paradox may, for the single individual, easily be confounded with a spiritual trial, is true enough; but for that reason one ought not to conceal it. That the whole inward fabric of many a man may be such that it repels him, is true enough; but for that reason one ought not to make faith into something other, in order to be able likewise to have it, but rather confess that one hath it not — while those who have faith ought to bethink them of setting up some marks, that one might distinguish the paradox from a spiritual trial.

The story of Abraham containeth, then, just such a teleological suspension of the ethical. There hath been no lack of acute heads and thorough scholars who have found analogies thereto. Their wisdom runneth out into the fine proposition that fundamentally everything is the same. If one will look a little more closely, I very much doubt that one shall find in the whole world a single analogy, save a later one, which proveth nothing — when it standeth fast that Abraham representeth faith, and that this is normally expressed in him, whose life is not only the most paradoxical that may be thought, but so paradoxical that it cannot be thought at all. He acteth by virtue of the absurd; for it is precisely the absurd that he, as the single individual, is higher than the universal. This paradox cannot be mediated; for as soon as he begineth thereon, he must confess that he was in a spiritual trial; and if this be so, he never cometh to sacrifice Isaac; or if he have sacrificed Isaac, then must he, repenting, return back to the universal. By virtue of the absurd he getteth Isaac again. Abraham, therefore, is at no moment a tragic hero, but something quite other — either a murderer, or a believer. The mediating term which saveth the tragic hero, Abraham hath not. Therefore is it that I can understand a tragic hero, but cannot understand Abraham — though in a certain demented sense I admire him more than all others.

Abraham's relation to Isaac, ethically expressed, is quite simply this, that the father shall love the son higher than himself. Yet the ethical hath, within its own compass, several gradations; let us see whether in this story there is to be found any such higher expression of the ethical, which can ethically explain his behavior, ethically warrant him in suspending the ethical obligation toward the son, without thereby moving out beyond the teleology of the ethical.

When an undertaking which is the concern of a whole people is hindered, when such an enterprise is stayed by Heaven's disfavor, when the wrathful divinity sendeth a calm that mocks every exertion, when the soothsayer accomplisheth his heavy office and proclaimeth that the god demandeth a young maiden as offering — then shall the father bring this offering with the courage of a hero. Magnanimously shall he hide his pain, though he might wish that he were “the lowly man who dare to weep,” not the king who must act royally. And though grief presseth solitarily into his breast, and he have but three confidants among the people, soon shall the whole people be confidant of his pain, but also confidant of his deed — that for the welfare of the whole he was willing to offer her, the daughter, the young and lovely maiden. O bosom! O fair cheeks, O flaxen hair (v. 687.). And the daughter shall move him with her tears, and the father shall turn away his countenance, but the hero shall lift the knife. — When then the tidings thereof reach the paternal home, then shall Greece's lovely maidens blush with enthusiasm, and if the daughter were betrothed, then shall the betrothed not be wroth, but be proud to take part in the father's deed, because the maiden belonged to him more tenderly than she belonged to the father.

When the bold judge who saved Israel in the hour of need bindeth, in one breath, God and himself by the same vow, then shall he heroically transform the young maiden's jubilation, the beloved daughter's joy, into sorrow, and all Israel shall mourn with her over her virgin youth; but every freeborn man shall understand, every stout-hearted woman shall admire Jephthah, and every maiden in Israel shall wish to act as did his daughter; for what would it have profited that Jephthah won by his vow, if he kept it not? Should not the victory then be taken away again from the people?

When a son forgetteth his duty, when the State entrusteth the father with the sword of judgment, when the laws demand the punishment from the father's hand, then shall the father heroically forget that the guilty one is his son; magnanimously shall he hide his pain, but there shall not be one in the people, not even the son, who doth not admire the father; and every time Rome's laws are interpreted, it shall be remembered that many have interpreted them more learnedly, but none more gloriously, than Brutus.

If, on the contrary, Agamemnon — while a favoring wind bore the fleet under full sail toward its goal — would have despatched that messenger who fetched Iphigenia, in order to sacrifice her; if Jephthah, without being bound by any vow which decided the people's destiny, would have said unto his daughter: “Mourn now for two months over thy brief youth, for I will sacrifice thee”; if Brutus had had a righteous son, and yet would have called upon the lictors to put him to death — who then should have understood them? If these three men, upon the question why they did this thing, had answered, “It is a trial wherein we are tried,” would one then have understood them better?

When Agamemnon, Jephthah, Brutus, in the decisive moment, heroically overcometh his pain, hath heroically lost the beloved, and hath but to consummate the deed outwardly, then shall there never be a noble soul in the world but hath the tears of compassion for their pain, and tears of admiration for their deed. If, on the contrary, these three men in the decisive moment would adjoin to the heroism wherewith they bore their pain the little phrase, “but it shall not, after all, take place” — who then should understand them? If as an explanation they added, “We believe it by virtue of the absurd,” who then should better understand them? — for who should not easily understand that it was absurd? But who should understand that one could then believe it?

The difference between the tragic hero and Abraham is easily perceived. The tragic hero remaineth still within the ethical. He letteth one expression of the ethical have its τέλος in a higher expression of the ethical; he reduceth the ethical relation between father and son, or between daughter and father, to a feeling that hath its dialectic in its relation to the idea of morality. There can therefore be no question here of a teleological suspension of the ethical itself.

With Abraham it standeth otherwise. By his deed he overstepped the whole of the ethical, and had a higher τέλος without it, in relation to which he suspended this. For I should yet very much like to know how one will bring Abraham's deed into relation with the universal, whether there can be discovered any kind of contact whatsoever between that which Abraham did and the universal, save this, that Abraham transgressed it. It is not in order to save a people, not in order to maintain the idea of the State, that Abraham doth it; not in order to reconcile angry gods. Could there be talk of the deity's being angered, then was He angered only with Abraham; and the whole of Abraham's deed standeth in no relation to the universal — it is a purely private undertaking. Whereas, therefore, the tragic hero is great by his moral virtue, Abraham is great by a purely personal virtue. There is no higher expression for the ethical in Abraham's life than this, that the father shall love the son. Of the ethical in the meaning of the moral there can simply be no question. Insofar as the universal was present, it was wrapped up in Isaac, hidden, so to speak, in Isaac's loins, and must therefore cry out with Isaac's mouth: “Do it not — thou art annihilating all.”

Wherefore, then, doth Abraham do it? For God's sake, and quite identically therewith, for his own sake. For God's sake he doth it, because God demandeth this proof of his faith; for his own sake he doth it, that he may furnish the proof. The unity of the two is quite rightly expressed in the word by which one hath always designated this relation: it is a trial, a temptation. A temptation; but what doth this mean? That which else tempteth a man is that which would hold him back from doing his duty; but here the temptation is the ethical itself, which would hold him back from doing God's will. But what then is duty? Duty is precisely the expression of God's will.

Here showeth itself the necessity of a new category for the understanding of Abraham. Such a relation to the deity, heathendom knoweth not. The tragic hero entereth into no private relation with the deity; rather, the ethical is the divine, and therefore the paradox in him letteth itself be mediated in the universal.

Abraham cannot be mediated, which may also be expressed thus: he cannot speak. As soon as I speak, I express the universal; and when I do not, then can no one understand me. As soon, then, as Abraham would express himself in the universal, he must say that his situation is a spiritual trial; for he hath no higher expression of the universal which standeth above the universal that he transgresseth.

Whereas, therefore, Abraham awakeneth my admiration, he likewise terrifieth me. He who denieth himself and sacrificeth himself for duty, he giveth up the finite in order to grasp the infinite; he is sure enough. The tragic hero giveth up the certain for the still more certain, and the spectator's eye resteth securely upon him. But he who giveth up the universal in order to grasp something still higher which is not the universal — what is he doing? Is it possible that this can be aught but a spiritual trial? And if it be possible, but the single individual then went astray, what salvation is there for him? He sufferreth the whole pain of the tragic hero; he annihilateth his joy in the world; he renounceth all things; and perhaps, in the same instant, he barreth himself from that exalted joy which was so dear to him that he would have purchased it at any price. Him the spectator can in no wise understand, neither securely let his eye rest upon him. Perhaps it cannot be done at all, that which the believer intendeth, since indeed it is unthinkable. Or if it could be done — if the single individual had misunderstood the deity — what salvation were there then for him? The tragic hero needeth tears, and he demandeth tears; and where was the envious eye so barren that it could not weep with Agamemnon? But where was he whose soul was so deluded that he presumed to weep over Abraham? The tragic hero accomplisheth his deed in a definite moment of time; but in the course of the times he doth that which is no less — he visiteth him whose soul is encompassed by sorrow, whose breast cannot get air for stifled sighs, whose thoughts hang heavy upon him, pregnant with tears; he showeth himself unto him, he lifteth the spell of sorrow, he looseneth the corslet, he allureth forth the tear, as the sufferer forgetteth his sufferings in his own. Over Abraham one cannot weep. One draweth nigh unto him with a horror religiosus, as Israel drew nigh unto Mount Sinai. — If, then, the solitary man who climbeth Mount Moriah, whose peak towereth sky-high above the plains of Aulis — if he be not a sleepwalker who walketh securely over the abyss, while he who standeth at the foot of the mountain and looketh thereon trembleth with anguish, and from reverence and horror dareth not even call unto him — if he becometh confused within himself, if he had taken the wrong way! — Thanks! and thanks again be unto him who reacheth out unto him whom life's sorrows have assailed and left naked, who reacheth unto him the expression, the leaf of the word, wherewith he may cover his wretchedness! Thanks be unto thee, great Shakespeare, thou who canst say everything, everything, everything precisely as it is — and yet wherefore didst thou never utter this anguish? Didst thou perhaps reserve it for thyself? as the beloved whose name one cannot even endure that the world should name; for a poet purchaseth this power of the word, to utter all the heavy secrets of others, at the price of a little secret which he cannot utter; and a poet is not an apostle — he casteth out devils only by the power of the devil.

But when the ethical is in this wise teleologically suspended, how then doth the single individual in whom it is suspended exist? He existeth as the single individual in opposition to the universal. Doth he then sin? For this is the form of sin, viewed in the idea, in such a way that, even though the child sinneth not, because it is not conscious of its existence as such, yet its existence, viewed in the idea, is sin, and the ethical demandeth itself of it at every moment. Should one deny that this form may be repeated in such a way that it is not sin, then judgment is passed upon Abraham. How then did Abraham exist? He believed. This is the paradox by which he keepeth upon the peak, which he cannot make plain to any other; for the paradox is, that he, as the single individual, setteth himself in an absolute relation to the absolute. Is he justified? His justification is again the paradox; for if he be, he is so not by virtue of being something universal, but by virtue of being the single individual.

How then doth the single individual assure himself that he is justified? It is easy enough to level the whole of existence upon the idea of the State, or upon the idea of society. If one doth this, then can one also easily mediate; for then one cometh not at all to the paradox, that the single individual as the single individual is higher than the universal — which I can also pertinently express in a saying of Pythagoras: that the odd number is more perfect than the even. Insofar as one occasionally in our age heareth an answer in the

direction of the paradox, it runneth commonly thus: it is to be judged by the outcome. A hero who hath become his contemporaries' σκάνδαλον, in the consciousness that he is a paradox who cannot make himself understood, calleth confidently to his contemporaries: the outcome shall surely prove that I was justified. In our age one heareth this cry more rarely; for as it bringeth forth no heroes (which is its defect), so it hath this good thing about it, that it bringeth forth also few caricatures. When, then, one heareth in our age these words, “it shall be judged by the outcome,” one is at once clear concerning whom one hath the honor of speaking with. They who speak thus are a numerous tribe, whom under one common name I will call the Docents. They live in their thoughts secured in existence; they have a fixed station and certain prospects in a well-ordered State; they have centuries, or even millennia, between themselves and the convulsions of existence; they fear not that the like may be repeated — what would the police and the newspapers say? Their work in life is to judge the great, and to judge them by the outcome. Such conduct toward the great betrayeth a singular mixture of arrogance and wretchedness — arrogance, because one deemeth oneself called to judge; wretchedness, because one feeleth not one's life even in the remotest degree akin to that of the great. Whoever is but a little erectioris ingenii, he hath yet not become an entirely cold and clammy mollusk; and as he draweth near unto the great, it can never depart from his mind that, since the creation of the world, it hath been the wont and use that the outcome cometh last, and that, when one is in truth to learn anything from the great, one must precisely give heed to the beginning. If he who is to act would judge himself by the outcome, then doth he never come to begin. Though the outcome may delight the whole world, yet can it not help the hero; for the outcome he learned of only when the whole was over, and not thereby did he become a hero — but a hero he was by this, that he began.

Furthermore, the outcome (insofar as it is finitude's answer to the infinite question) is in its dialectic altogether disparate with the hero's existence. Or shall it be able to prove that Abraham was justified in conducting himself as the single individual over against the universal, that he by a miracle received Isaac back? Had Abraham really sacrificed Isaac, would he therefore have been less justified?

But the outcome one is curious about, as one is curious about the outcome of a book; the anguish, the distress, the paradox — of these one will know nothing. With the outcome one dallieth aesthetically; it cometh as unexpectedly, but also as easily, as a prize in the lottery; and when one hath heard the outcome, then hath one edified oneself. And yet no temple-robber, who toils in chains and irons, is so base a malefactor as he who thus plundereth the holy; and Judas, who sold his Lord for thirty pieces of silver, is not more contemptible than he who thus selleth the great.

It is against my soul to speak inhumanly of the great, to let it dim itself at a vast distance in indeterminate shape, to let it be great without yet the human in it coming forth, whereby it ceaseth to be great; for not what befalleth me maketh me great, but what I do; and surely there is no one who supposeth that a man became great because he won the great prize in the lottery. Even though a man were born in lowly circumstances, I require of him still that he be not so inhuman against himself as to be unable to conceive the king's castle save at a distance, and to dream indefinitely of its grandeur, and at one and the same time wish to exalt it and abolish it by exalting it in a base manner; I require of him that he be man enough to come forth thither also confidently and with dignity. He shall not be unman enough to wish, in unmannerly wise, to violate all things, by storming straight from the street into the king's halls — by such a course he loseth more than the king; on the contrary, he shall find a joy in observing every command of seemliness with a glad and trustful enthusiasm, which precisely shall make him bold of heart. This is but an image; for that distinction is but a most imperfect expression of the spirit's distance. I require of every man that he think not so inhumanly of himself that he dare not enter into those palaces where not only the memory of the chosen dwelleth, but where they themselves dwell. He shall not unmannerly thrust himself forward and force upon them his kinship; he shall be blessed every time he boweth himself before them; but he shall be confident and bold of heart, and ever something more than a charwoman; for if he will not be more, then doth he never come thither. And that which is to help him is precisely the anguish and the distress wherein the great are tried; for else, if he have any marrow in him at all, these would only awaken his righteous envy. And that which can only be great at a distance, that which by means of empty and hollow phrases one would make into something great — that one oneself annihilateth.

Who was great in the world as that highly favored woman, the mother of God, the Virgin Mary? And yet how doth one speak of her? That she was the favored one among women maketh her not great; and were it not so curiously the case that those who hear can think just as inhumanly as those who speak, then surely every young maiden must ask, “Wherefore did not I also become the favored one?” And had I nothing else to say, I should not at all dismiss such a question as foolish; for in respect of a favor, abstractly considered, every man is equally entitled. They leave out the distress, the anguish, the paradox. My thought is as pure as any man's; and he who can think such a thing, his thought shall surely be pure — and he hath also the dreadful to await, if it be not so; for he who once hath had these

images come before him, he cannot get rid of them again, and if he sin against them, then do they avenge themselves dreadfully with a still wrath, more dreadful than the loud outcry of ten ravenous reviewers. Truly, Mary bore the child miraculously, but yet it went with her after the manner of women; and that time, it is the time of anguish, of distress, and of the paradox. The angel was indeed a ministering spirit, but he was not an officious spirit who went unto the other young maidens in Israel and said, “Despise not Mary, unto her befalleth the extraordinary.” But the angel came only unto Mary, and no one could understand her. What woman was ever so injured as Mary? And is it not also true here, that he whom God blesseth, He cursed in the same breath? This is the spirit's apprehension of Mary; and she is by no means — what it offendeth me to say, but yet more, that one hath thoughtlessly and dallyingly so apprehended her — she is by no means a lady who sitteth in state and playeth with a divine child. When she nevertheless said, “Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord,” then is she great, and I think it shall not fall out hard to explain wherefore she became the mother of God. She needeth no worldly admiration, as little as Abraham needeth tears; for she was not a heroine, and he was not a hero, but neither of them became greater than these by being exempted from the distress and the agony and the paradox — they became so by these.

It is a great thing, when the poet, while he placeth his tragic hero before men's admiration, dare say, “Weep over him, for he hath deserved it”; for it is a great thing to deserve the tears of those who deserve to shed tears; it is a great thing that the poet dare hold the multitude in check, dare chastise men, that every man may prove himself, whether he be worthy to weep over the hero — for the slop-water of blubberers is a degradation of the holy. — Yet greater than all this is it, that the knight of faith dare say even unto the noble man who would weep over him, “Weep not over me, but weep over thyself.”

One is moved; one seeketh oneself back into those beautiful times; sweet, langourous longings lead one to the wish's goal: to behold Christ wandering about in the promised land. One forgetteth the anguish, the distress, the paradox. Was it then so easy a matter not to take the wrong way? Was it not dreadful that this man, who walked among the others, that he was God? Was it not dreadful to sit at table with him? Was it then so easy a matter to become an apostle? But the outcome, eighteen centuries — that helpeth, that helpeth toward this paltry deceit wherewith one deceiveth oneself and others. I feel not courage to wish to be contemporary with such events; but for that reason I judge not strictly of those who took the wrong way, nor meanly of those who saw rightly.
Yet I return unto Abraham. In the time before the outcome, Abraham was either at every minute a murderer, or we stand at the paradox which is higher than all mediations.

Abraham's history containeth, then, a teleological suspension of the ethical. He hath, as the single individual, become higher than the universal. This is the paradox, which will not let itself be mediated. It is just as inexplicable how he came into it, as it is inexplicable how he abideth in it. If it stand not so with Abraham, then is he not even a tragic hero, but a murderer. To go on calling him the father of faith, to speak thereof unto men who care for nothing but words, is thoughtless. A tragic hero a man can become by his own powers, but the knight of faith he cannot. When a man entereth upon the in a certain sense heavy way of the tragic hero, then can many counsel him; he who walketh faith's narrow way, him can no man counsel, no man understand. Faith is a
wonder, and yet no man is excluded therefrom; for that wherein all human life is at one is in passion, and faith is a passion.

chapters.title: Problema II — Is there an Absolute Duty toward God?
paragraphs: The ethical is the universal, and as such, in turn, the divine. One is therefore right in saying that every duty is at bottom a duty toward God; but if one cannot say more, then one says at the same time that I, properly speaking, have no duty toward God. The duty becomes duty by being referred to God; but in the duty itself I do not enter into relation with God. Thus it is a duty to love one's neighbor. It is a duty by being referred to God, but in the duty I enter into relation, not with God, but with the neighbor whom I love. If, then, I say in this connection that it is my duty to love God, I am, properly speaking, only uttering a tautology, inasmuch as “God” is here taken in an entirely abstract sense as the divine, i.e., the universal, i.e., duty. The whole existence of the human race rounds itself off in itself perfectly as a sphere, and the ethical is at once that which limits and that which fills out. God becomes an invisible, vanishing point, an impotent thought; His power is only in the ethical, which fills out existence. So insofar as anyone should fall into wishing to love God in any other than the sense here indicated, then he is overstrained; he loves a phantom which, if it had only so much power that it could speak, would say to him: I do not require thy love; remain only where thou belongest. Insofar as anyone should fall into wishing to love God otherwise, then this love becomes suspect, like the love of which Rousseau speaks, wherewith a man loves the Kaffirs in lieu of loving his neighbor.

If, then, what has here been developed is correct, if there is nothing incommensurable in a human life, but the incommensurable that there is, is so only by an accident from which nothing follows insofar as existence is regarded under the idea — then Hegel is right; but he is not right in speaking of faith, or in permitting Abraham to be regarded as its father; for by the latter he has passed sentence both upon Abraham and upon faith. In the Hegelian philosophy *das Äussere* (*die Entäusserung*) is higher than *das Innere*. This is often illustrated by an example. The child is *das Innere*, the man *das Äussere*; whence it comes that the child is precisely determined by the outward, and conversely the man as *das Äussere* is precisely determined by *das Innere*. Faith, on the other hand, is this paradox, that inwardness is higher than outwardness — or, to recall once more an expression in the foregoing, that the odd number is higher than the even.

For the ethical view of life it is then the task of the single individual to strip himself of the determination of inwardness and to express this in an outward. Every time the single individual flinches from this, every time he wishes to hold back in, or slip down again into, the determination of inwardness — of feeling, mood, and the like — then he transgresses, then he lies in a spiritual trial. The paradox of faith is this, that there is an inwardness which is incommensurable with the outward, an inwardness which, mark well, is not identical with the first, but is a new

inwardness. This must not be overlooked. The newer philosophy has permitted itself, without further ado, to substitute for “faith” the immediate. When one does this, then it is a piece of ridiculousness to deny that faith has existed in all ages. Faith comes thus into rather plain company with feeling, mood, idiosyncrasy, *vapeurs*, and the like. To this extent philosophy may be in the right, that one ought not to remain at this point. But there is nothing that entitles philosophy to this use of language. Faith is preceded by a movement of infinity; only then does faith enter, *nec opinate*, by virtue of the absurd. This I can well understand, without therefore claiming that I have faith. If faith be nothing more than what philosophy gives it out to be, then Socrates already went further, far further, instead of the contrary, that he did not arrive at it. He has in an intellectual respect made the movement of infinity. His ignorance is the infinite resignation. This task is even now a fitting one for human powers, though our age scorns it; but only when it has been accomplished, only when the single individual has emptied himself in the infinite — only then has the point come where faith can break forth.

The paradox of faith, then, is this, that the single individual is higher than the universal, that the single individual — to recall a now rarer dogmatic distinction — determines his relation to the universal by his relation to the absolute, not his relation to the absolute by his relation to the universal. The paradox can also be expressed thus, that there is an absolute duty toward God; for in this relation of duty the single individual as the single individual relates himself absolutely to the absolute. So when in this connection it is said that it is duty to love God, then something other is said than in the foregoing; for if this duty is absolute, then the ethical is reduced to the relative. From this, however, it does not follow that the ethical shall be annulled; rather, it receives a quite different expression, the paradoxical expression, so that, for example, love to God may bring the knight of faith to give to his love of his neighbor the opposite expression of that which, ethically speaking, is duty.
If it be not so, then faith has not its place in existence; then faith is a spiritual trial, and Abraham is lost, since he gave way to it.

This paradox does not admit of mediation; for it rests precisely upon this, that the single individual is only the single individual. So soon as this single individual would express his absolute duty in the universal, would become conscious of it therein, then he recognizes that he is in a spiritual trial, and then, if he otherwise makes the resistance, he does not come to fulfil the so-called absolute duty; and if he does not, then he sins, even though his deed *realiter* should turn out to be that which was his absolute duty. What, then, was Abraham to do? If he had said to another man, “Isaac I love higher than all in the world, and therefore it is so heavy a thing for me to sacrifice him,” the other would surely have shaken his head and said, “Why then wilt thou sacrifice him?” — or, if the other had been a shrewd head, he would surely even have seen through Abraham, that he was making a parade of feelings which stood in a heaven-crying contradiction with his deed.

In the story of Abraham we find such a paradox. His relation to Isaac, ethically expressed, is this, that the father shall love the son. This ethical relation is reduced to the relative in opposition to the absolute relation to God. To the question, Why? Abraham has no other answer than that it is a trial, a temptation, which, as remarked above, is the unity of being for God's sake and for his own sake. These two determinations correspond also to each other in linguistic usage. Thus when one sees a man do something which does not enter into the universal, one says, that he hardly did it for God's sake, signifying thereby that he did it for his own sake. The paradox of faith has lost the middle term, i.e., the universal. On the one hand it has the expression of the highest egoism (doing the dreadful deed which it does for its own sake); on the other hand the expression of the most absolute self-surrender, doing it for God's sake. Faith itself cannot be mediated into the universal; for thereby it is annulled. Faith is this paradox, and the single individual cannot at all make himself intelligible to anyone. One imagines, perhaps, that the single individual can make himself intelligible to another single individual who is in the same case. Such a notion would be unthinkable, were it not that in our age in so many ways one seeks to slink slyly into the great. The one knight of faith cannot help the other at all. Either the single individual himself becomes a knight of faith by taking the paradox upon himself, or he never becomes one. Companionship in these regions is altogether unthinkable. Any closer explication of what is to be understood by Isaac the single individual can constantly give only to himself. And though one were able, in general terms, never so precisely to define what should be understood by Isaac (which moreover would be the most ridiculous self-contradiction, to bring the single individual, who precisely stands outside the universal, under universal definitions, when he is to act precisely as the single individual who is outside the universal), yet the single individual would never be able to assure himself thereof through others, but only through himself as the single individual. Therefore, even were a man cowardly and wretched enough to wish to become a knight of faith on another's word and warrant, he yet does not become one; for only the single individual becomes such as the single individual, and this is the great thing, which I can well understand without entering into it, since I lack the courage; but this is also the dreadful thing, which I can still better

comprehend. There is set forth, as is well known, in Luke xiv. 26, a remarkable doctrine concerning the absolute duty toward God: “If any man come to me, and hate not his own father, and his mother, and his wife, and his children, and his brothers and his sisters, yea, and his own soul also, he cannot be my disciple.” This is a hard saying; who can bear to hear it? On that account it is also very seldom heard. Yet this silence is only a subterfuge that helps not at all. The student of theology, however, comes to learn that these words occur in the New Testament, and in some exegetical aid he finds the information that *misein* in this and a couple of other passages stands per *meiosin* for: *minus diligo, posthabeo, non colo, nihili facio*. The connection in which these words occur, however, does not seem to confirm this tasteful explanation. For in the very next verse there is a story of how one who would build a tower first makes an estimate, whether he be able to do it, lest afterwards men should laugh at him. The close connection of this story with the cited verse seems precisely to indicate that the words are to be taken as terribly as possible, in order that everyone may try himself, whether he be able to erect the building.

If that pious and tender-hearted exegete, who by such haggling thinks to smuggle Christianity into the world, should have the good fortune to convince a man that this was, both grammatically and linguistically and *kat' analogian*, the meaning of that passage, then he will, it is to be hoped, have the good fortune in the same instant to convince that same man that Christianity is one of the most miserable things in the world. For that doctrine, which in one of its most lyrical outbursts, where the consciousness of its eternal validity swells most strongly within it, has nothing else to say than a clamorous word that means nothing, but only signifies that one is to be less benevolent, less attentive, more indifferent — that doctrine which, the moment it makes a face as though it would say the dreadful thing, ends with cooling instead of terrifying — that doctrine is surely not worth standing up for.

The words are dreadful, yet I think one may well understand them, without it following therefrom that he who has understood them therefore has the courage to do it. So honest one ought to be, however, that one acknowledges what stands there, that one confesses that it is the great thing, even though one have not oneself the courage for it. He who bears himself thus shall not exclude himself from participation in the beautiful story; for it does, after a fashion, contain consolation for him who had not the courage to begin upon the building of the tower. But honest he must be, and not explain this lack of courage as humility, since on the contrary it is pride, whereas the courage of faith is the only humble courage.

It is now easy to perceive that, if there is to be any meaning in the passage, it must be understood quite literally. God is He who demands absolute love. He who, in demanding a man's love, would suppose that this love should also prove itself by his becoming lukewarm to all that was otherwise dear to him — he is not only an egoist, he is also stupid; and he who would demand such a love, in the same instant signs his own death-warrant, insofar as he had his life in the love so coveted. Thus a man demands that his wife shall leave father and mother; but if he should regard it as a proof of her extraordinary love for him, that for his sake she became a lukewarm and listless daughter, and so on, then he is more stupid than the most stupid. Had he any conception of what love is, he would wish to discover, and
to behold therein, an assurance that his wife would love him as none other in the kingdom, if he discovered that as a daughter and sister she was perfect in love.
What one would, then, in a man regard as a sign
of egoism and stupidity, that one is, with the help of an exegete, to regard as a worthy conception of the Deity.

But how, then, is one to hate them? I shall here not recall the human distinction, either to love or to hate; not because I have so much against it, for it is at any rate passionate, but because it is egoistic and does not fit here. If, on the other hand, I regard the task as a paradox, then I understand it, i.e., I understand it as one can understand a paradox. The absolute duty can then bring one to do what the ethical would forbid, but it can by no means bring the knight of faith to leave off loving. This Abraham shows. The instant he is about to sacrifice Isaac, the ethical expression for what he does is this: he hates Isaac. But if he really hated Isaac, he could be at peace that God did not require this of him; for Cain and Abraham are not identical. Isaac he must love with his whole soul; when God demands him, he must love him, if possible, even higher, and only then can he sacrifice him; for it is precisely this love to Isaac which, by its paradoxical opposition to his love to God, makes his deed a sacrifice. But this is the distress and the anguish in the paradox, that, humanly speaking, he cannot at all make himself intelligible. Only at the instant when his deed is in absolute contradiction with his feeling, only then does he sacrifice Isaac; but the reality of his deed is that whereby he belongs to the universal, and there he is and remains a murderer.

The passage in Luke must furthermore be so understood that one perceives that the knight of faith obtains no higher expression whatsoever of the universal (such as the ethical) wherein he can save himself. So when one let the Church demand this sacrifice of one of its members, then we have only a tragic hero. For the idea of the Church is not qualitatively different from that of the State, so soon as the single individual can come into it by a simple mediation; and so soon as the

single individual has entered into the paradox, he does not come to the idea of the Church; he does not come out of the paradox, but must either find his blessedness therein, or his perdition. Such an ecclesiastical hero expresses in his deed the universal, and there shall be no one in the Church, not even his father and mother and so on, without their understanding him. The knight of faith, on the other hand, he is not, and has also another answer than Abraham's; he does not say that it is a trial or a temptation wherein he is being tried.

One generally refrains from citing such passages as that in Luke. One fears to let men loose; one fears that the worst will happen, when first the single individual is pleased to *gerere* himself as the single individual. Furthermore, one supposes that to exist as the single individual is the easiest of all, and therefore one must precisely constrain men to become the universal. I can share neither that fear nor this opinion, and that for the same reason. He who has learned that to exist as the single individual is the most dreadful of all shall not be afraid to say that it is the greatest, but he shall also say it in such wise that his words hardly become a snare for one who has gone astray, but rather help him into the universal, even though his words make a little room for the great. He who dares not name such passages, dares not name Abraham either; and to suppose that to exist as the single individual is easy enough contains a very questionable indirect concession with respect to oneself; for he who really has reverence for himself and concern for his soul is assured that the man who lives under his own oversight, alone in the whole world, lives more strictly and recluse than a maiden in her bower. That there may be those who need compulsion, those who, were they set at liberty, would like ungovernable beasts riot in selfish lust, is well true; but one shall precisely show that one does not belong to them, by the fact that one knows how to speak with anxiety and trembling; and speak one must, out of reverence for the great, that it be not forgotten for fear of the harm — which surely will not come, when one speaks in such a way that one knows it is the great thing, knows its terrors; and without this one neither knows its greatness.

Let us now consider a little more closely the distress and the anguish in the paradox of faith. The tragic hero resigns himself in order to express the universal; the knight of faith resigns the universal in order to become the single individual. As I have said, all depends upon how one is situated. He who supposes that it is easy enough to be the single individual can always be sure that he is no knight of faith; for loose birds and vagabond geniuses are not men of faith. The knight of faith, on the other hand, knows that it is glorious to belong to the universal. He knows that it is beautiful and beneficent to be the single individual who translates himself into the universal — he who, so to speak, himself takes care of producing a clean and elegant and so far as possible faultless edition of himself, legible by all; he knows that it is refreshing to become intelligible to oneself in the universal, in such a way that he understands it, and every single individual who understands him understands the universal anew in him, and both rejoice in the security of the universal. He knows that it is beautiful to be born as the single individual who has his home in the universal, his friendly abiding-place, which at once receives him with open arms when he wills to remain in it. But he knows likewise that higher than this there twists a lonely path, narrow and steep; he knows that it is dreadful to be born solitary out of the universal, to walk without meeting a single wayfarer. He knows very well where he is, and how he stands related to men. Humanly speaking, he is mad and cannot make himself intelligible to anyone. And yet to be mad is the mildest expression. If he is not regarded thus, then he is a hypocrite, and the higher he climbs upon the way, the more dreadful a hypocrite.

The knight of faith knows that it is inspiring to give oneself up for the universal, that there belongs courage thereto, but that there is also a security therein, precisely because it is for the universal; he knows that it is glorious to be understood by every noble soul, and so understood that the beholder himself is ennobled thereby. This he knows, and he feels himself as it were bound; he could wish that this were the task that had been set him. So Abraham could surely now and then have wished that the task were to love Isaac as it behooves a father, intelligible to all, unforgettable through the ages; he could wish that the task were to sacrifice Isaac for the universal, that he might inspire fathers to glorious deeds — and he is almost terrified at the thought that for him such wishes are only spiritual trials, and must be treated as such; for he knows that it is a lonely way he treads, and that he accomplishes nothing for the universal, but is only being tested and tried himself. Or what did Abraham accomplish for the universal? Let me speak humanly thereof, quite humanly! He uses seventy years to obtain a son of his old age. What others get quickly enough and have joy of long, this he uses seventy years to obtain; and wherefore? because he is being tried and tempted. Is it not madness! But Abraham believed, and only Sarah wavered and got him to take Hagar to be a concubine; but for that reason also he had to drive her away. He gets Isaac — then he is to be tried again. He knew that it is glorious to express the universal, glorious to live with Isaac. But that is not the task. He knew that it is kingly to sacrifice such a son for the universal; he himself should have found rest therein, and all should have rested in praise of his deed, as the vowel rests in its silent letter; but that is not the task — he is being tried. That Roman commander who is famous by his cognomen

Cunctator stayed the foe by his hesitation — but what a hesitator is Abraham in comparison with him! and yet he saves not the State. This is the content of one hundred and thirty years. Who can endure it? Should not his contemporaries, if there could be any question of such, say: “It is an everlasting hesitation with Abraham; at length he got a son, that lasted long enough; now he will sacrifice him — is he not deranged? And could he but explain why he wills it; but it is always a trial.” More Abraham could not explain either; for his life is as a book laid under divine seal, which becomes not *publici juris*.

This is the dreadful thing. He who does not see this can always be sure that he is no knight of faith; but he who sees it shall not deny that even the most tested tragic hero walks as in a dance, in comparison with the knight of faith, who only comes forward slowly and creeping. And when he has perceived this and assured himself that he has not the courage to understand it, then will he perhaps divine the wondrous glory which that knight attains, that he becomes God's confidant, the Friend of the Lord — to speak quite humanly — that he says *Du* to God in heaven, while even the tragic hero only addresses Him in the third person.

The tragic hero is soon finished, and has soon fought his fight; he makes the infinite movement and is now secure in the universal. The knight of faith, on the other hand, is kept sleepless; for he is constantly being tried, and at every instant there is a possibility of being able to return repentant to the universal, and this possibility may just as well be a spiritual trial as truth. Concerning this he can fetch information from no man; for so he is outside the paradox.

The knight of faith has, then, first and foremost, the passion to concentrate the entire ethical, with which he is breaking, into a single moment, that he may be able to give himself the assurance that he really loves Isaac with his whole soul. If he cannot do this, then he lies in a spiritual trial. Next, he has the passion in an instant to bring forth this entire assurance, and that in such wise that it is just as fully valid as in the first moment. If he cannot do this, then he never gets from the spot; for then he must be constantly beginning anew. The tragic hero also concentrates the ethical, beyond which he teleologically went, into a single moment, but he has in this respect a foothold in the universal. The knight of faith has only and alone himself, and therein lies the dreadful thing. Most men live in an ethical obligation in such wise that they let each day have its sorrow, but then also they never come to this passionate concentration, this energetic consciousness. Toward the obtaining of this the universal can in a certain sense be of help to the tragic hero; but the knight of faith is alone with

all. The tragic hero does it, and finds rest in the universal; the knight of faith is constantly held in tension. Agamemnon gives up Iphigenia and has thereby found rest in the universal; he now proceeds to sacrifice her. Had Agamemnon not made the movement, had his soul in the decisive moment, instead of passionate concentration, been lost in common prattle that he had several daughters, and that *vielleicht* yet *das Ausserordentliche* might happen — then is he naturally no hero, but a hospital-inmate. The hero's concentration Abraham also has, even though in him it is far more difficult, since he has no foothold whatever in the universal; but he makes one further movement, by which he gathers his soul back upon the wonder. Had Abraham not done this, then is he only an Agamemnon — insofar, that is, as one can otherwise explain how it is to be defended that one would sacrifice Isaac, when one does not thereby benefit the universal.

Whether the single individual really lies in a spiritual trial, or whether he is a knight of faith, this only the single individual himself can decide. Yet there might out of the paradox be constructed some marks which also he may understand who is not within it. The true knight of faith is always the absolute isolation; the spurious is sectarian. This latter is an attempt to leap off from the narrow way of the paradox and become a tragic hero on the cheap. The tragic hero expresses the universal and sacrifices himself for it. Instead of this, the sectarian Master Jakel has a private theatre, a few good friends and comrades, who about as well represent the universal as the staff-bearers in *The Golden Snuffbox* represent justice. The knight of faith, on the contrary, he is the paradox, he is the single individual, absolutely the single individual, without any connections or wide-ranging affiliations. This is the dreadful thing, which the sectarian wretch cannot endure. Instead, that is, of learning therefrom that he is not capable of doing the great thing, and then frankly confessing this — something which I, of course, can only approve, since it is what I myself do — the bungler thinks that by joining together with some other bunglers he shall be able to do it. But it goes by no means; in the world of the spirit no swindling is suffered. A dozen sectarians take each other under the arm; they know nothing at all of the lonely spiritual trials which await the knight of faith, and which he dare not flee, precisely because it would be still more dreadful, did he presumptuously press himself forward. The sectarians drown one another out with noise and clamor, hold off anguish by their shouting; and such a hooting Deer-park company supposes that it is taking heaven by storm, and supposes that it is going by the same way as the knight of faith, who in the loneliness of the universe never hears any human voice, but walks alone with his dreadful responsibility.

The knight of faith is referred to himself alone; he feels the pain that he cannot make himself intelligible to others, but he feels no vain desire to wish to instruct others. The pain is to him the assurance; the vain desire he knows not, for thereto is he too earnest of soul. The spurious knight betrays himself easily by this mastery, which he has acquired in a moment. He grasps not at all what the matter is, namely, that, insofar as another single individual is to walk the same way, he must in altogether the same manner become the single individual, and then needs no man's guidance, least of all that of one who would obtrude himself. Here, again, one leaps off; one cannot endure the martyrdom of unintelligibility, and instead of this one chooses, conveniently enough, the worldly admiration of mastery. The true knight of faith is a witness, never a teacher, and therein lies the deep humanity, which is worth more than this prating sympathy with other men's woes and weals, which is honored under the name of sympathy, while it is yet nothing else than vanity. He who would be only a witness thereby confesses that no man, not even the lowliest, has need of another man's sympathy, or shall be debased thereby, in order that another may be exalted. But as he himself did not win what he won at a cheap price, so neither does he sell it out cheaply; he is not wretched enough to take men's admiration and in return give them his silent contempt; he knows that what is in truth great is alike accessible to all.

Either, then, there is an absolute duty toward God; and if there is such, then it is the paradox here described, that the single individual as the single individual is higher than the universal, and as the single individual stands in an absolute relation to the absolute — or else there has never been faith, because it has always existed; or else Abraham is lost; or else one must explain the passage in Luke xiv. as that tasteful exegete did, and in like manner explain the corresponding passages, and the like.
